A rift is a crack, split, or gap that forms when something that was once whole or connected breaks apart. The word works in two main ways — one physical, one about people and relationships — but the same central idea runs through both: something that was joined together has been torn open.

In the physical world, a rift is a long, deep crack in the earth, rock, or ice. Imagine pulling a piece of bread apart with your hands — that tear, that opening, is the idea behind a rift. In geology, when two sections of the earth's crust are pulled away from each other, the crack that forms between them is called a rift. The Great Rift Valley in East Africa is one of the most famous examples in the world — a massive, dramatic split in the earth's surface running thousands of kilometers. You can also say "a rift in the clouds," meaning a gap or break in the cloud cover where light comes through.
The relational meaning — and this is where the word truly lives

This is the meaning you will encounter most often. A rift between people or groups refers to a serious, deep breakdown in a relationship. It is not just a small disagreement or a momentary argument. A rift means that something fundamental has cracked — trust, loyalty, or a bond that once held two people or groups together.

When a rift develops between two friends, it means they have grown apart in a way that feels real and significant, like a visible gap has opened between them. When there is a rift between two countries, it means their relationship has deteriorated seriously — alliances have weakened, trust has broken down, and there is now tension and distance where there was once cooperation.

The word carries genuine emotional weight. It signals that the damage is not superficial. A minor disagreement is not a rift. A rift is what remains after hurt, betrayal, or prolonged conflict has left a lasting mark.
How serious is a rift? Is it permanent?

A rift is serious, but it is not automatically permanent — and this is one of the most important things to understand about the word. You can heal a rift, mend a rift, or bridge a rift. These phrases mean repairing the broken relationship and closing the gap. However, a rift that is ignored or left unaddressed tends to grow wider over time, like a crack in a wall that spreads if you never fix it. Whether a rift becomes permanent depends on whether the people involved choose to repair it.
How rift differs from similar words

A disagreement is just a difference of opinion — two people see something differently. A dispute is a more active conflict, often about a specific issue. A falling out is a fight or argument that damaged a relationship. A rift, on the other hand, is what the relationship looks like after that damage has settled in — the lasting divide, the visible gap, the structural fracture in what was once whole. It is deeper and more serious than all of these. If a disagreement is a scratch on wood, a rift is the wood splitting apart.
How the word is used in everyday language

You will often hear phrases like "a growing rift," which means the divide between two parties is getting worse over time. "A deep rift" signals that the divide is very serious. "A rift opened up between them" is a natural way of saying a divide began to form. "Heal the rift" or "bridge the rift" means to repair the relationship. You will almost always see the word paired with "between" — a rift between two people, a rift between nations, a rift between political parties.

Here are a few natural example sentences to tie it all together. Physical use: "The earthquake left a deep rift running across the valley floor." Relational use: "There has been a rift between the two brothers ever since their father's estate was divided." Political use: "The trade dispute created a serious rift between the two allied nations that took years to repair."

In summary, a rift is always a break — in the earth, in a relationship, or in trust. It is deeper than a simple disagreement, more lasting than a fight, and always suggests that something that was once connected has been pulled apart. When used about people, it carries the feeling that the gap between them is real, significant, and in need of deliberate effort to close.
